LOGIC OF CONCORD WITH COLLECTIVES IN BIBLICAL NARRATIVE*
UNIVERSITY OF TORONTO
body.p: 1. Introduction.

1.1 For the purposes of this study, collectives are defined as nouns which are morphologically singular, but which may have singular or plural coreferents. A coreferent of a collective is commonly described as showing “grammatical” concord when singular, “notional” concord (constructio ad sensum) when plural. If this is taken as indicating that concord is determined either by linguistic convention (a noun which is singular in form has singular coreferents) or by the speaker’s perception of reality (the plural is used to make reference to a collection of individ­ uals), a difficulty appears. A compound subject should have plural coreferents both according to grammatical convention, and as a reflection of reality, yet a compound subject of which the first component designates

1.2 There is regularity in the choice of number in the coreferents of collectives in one limited area. An attributive which presents a quality of the group designated by the collective (and not of the individuals which form it) is singular. As described, the basis of this is semantic, so the value of the term “grammatical” for such concord is questionable. Equally, one would expect that a speaker would be led to think of a group performing particular actions as a number of individuals rather than as a unit, and so to the “notional” use of a plural verb where the subject was a collective. It is true that an active verb with a collective subject is often plural, but there is no group of verbs which are charac­ teristically plural when the subject is collective. This might be held to show that the “notional” plural is a free variant of the “grammatical” singular, were it not that the use of the latter is, in one area at least, clearly conditioned.

1.3 This paper is an attempt to determine what the terms “grammatical” and “notional” represent when used in the way indicated. It is based on the books of Judges, Samuel, and Kings, but is limited to collectives which denote humans. This corpus provides some 400 cases in which a collective is subject of a verb, or is modified by an attributive, and so is marked for number, a sample large enough to provide a satisfactory basis for conclusions. The language of these books is homogeneous, and can reasonably be treated synchronically. The method of study is

2. Number and Transitivity.

2.1 When compared in terms of the number of the verb of which they are subject, the collectives denoting humans found in the corpus fall naturally into three groups in terms of the number of their coreferents.
1. The name Israel, and the names of the constituent tribes (and similar groups), are treated as plural in only two of the 45 possible cases (4%).

2. The lowest, gentilic designations, are plural in 3 of 9 cases (33%), the highest, the collective ‘man’ with a numerical modifier, in 8 of 17 cases (47%).

body.p: 2.2 The names in group (1) represent not only population groups, but also their eponymous ancestors. The groups themselves are often desig- nated as the descendants (םינב) of these ancestors, as ‘the descendants of Israel’, etc. The existence of plural designations equivalent to these collectives is no doubt the reason why the latter are usually treated as singular.9 Equivalent collective and plural designations of this sort do not appear to be free variants. The collective forms act as subject of a clause in less than 10% of their occurrences, the equivalent plurals in 50% or more. For instance ןימינב ‘Benjamin’ as a collective, acts as subject in the corpus in 4 of 48 possible cases (8%), ינב ‘the descendants of Benjamin’ in 12 of 22 cases (55%). There is, then, a relationship between the representation of a group as “actor” (subject) and the choice of plural number.

2.3 This tendency to treat a group as plural where it appears as “actor” is related to the transitivity of the clause. 3. Number and “Narrative Prominence.”

3.1 Clauses with collective subject show a similar correlation of tran- sitivity with plural number. Where a verb or participle acting as predicate is passive, stative or reflexive, it is nearly always singular where the subject is collective. Where the predicate indicates motion, the singular is less common. Where it indicates speech or perception, the predicate is often plural. This can be illustrated by a survey of the roots most commonly used in each group to head predicates with collective subjects. As with the survey in §2.5, the numbers in the “other active” column do not show the expected progression. Again, this is partly due to the exceptional character of Judg 11:13-21. If this passage were excluded, the figures for ‘take’ would be 2/5, those for ‘send’ 2/3: more in line with expectations. It is a fact, however, that collectives—or even plural nominals denoting groups of humans—are not often used with verbs of this group. If the reason were understood, we might also understand why the proportion of singular verbs with collective subjects is unex­ pectedly high in this group.

3.2 The correlation between high transitivity and the treatment of a collective as plural can be investigated more precisely in terms of the parameters of transitivity set up in P. J. Hopper and S. A. Thompson. 12 Such an investigation is, however, confronted with several problems. The limits of our knowledge of Biblical Hebrew would reduce treatment of parameters like “aspect” and “punctuality” largely to guesswork. In addition, the boundaries of semantic categories are typically ill-defined. Some examples are easy to assign to opposing categories, but for a considerable proportion, assignment can only be arbitrary, as would be the case if all humans were to be categorized as “tall” or “short.” Moreover, a variety of factors typically condition the choice between contrasting items which carry a semantic load, just as a number of factors, such as sex and diet, would affect human stature. It is easy enough to select examples to show that a particular factor is significant in some cases, but the conclusion that it is significant in all cases must be derived by argument. It cannot be demonstrated, because no one factor is always dominant.

body.p: 3.3 According to Hopper and Thompson’s study, a clause with only one participant is low in transitivity. Since low transitivity correlates with use of the singular, such a clause is likely to have a singular verb, as in
Sam Israel was driven back.
body.head: 1 Kgs All the people answered.
body.p: A clause with more than one participant, and so with higher transitivity, is likely to have a plural verb, as
Sam Israel was there driven back before David’s servants.
body.head: 1 Kgs The people answered him not a word.
body.p: According to Hopper and Thompson,14 a negative clause is lower in transitivity than an affirmative one. The verb of a negative clause with a collective subject is regularly singular in the corpus, even where the subject is given prominence, as
Sam The people did not know that Jonathan had gone.

The clause quoted from 1 Kgs 18:21 presents an exception. This may be because the number of participants gives it a high level of transitivity, but the evidence of the corpus is too limited to demonstrate this. There are too many variables for a detailed illustration of the correlation between plurality and transitivity through Hopper and Thompson’s pa- rameters to carry much weight. A general correlation between a high level of transitivity and the use of the plural is as much as can be established.
3.4 The use of the plural appears to be characteristic of clauses which are prominent in terms of narrative function. In some cases prominence
body.head: MAARAV9 (2002)
body.p: is marked through syntactic structure.15 In other cases it can only be inferred from the part played in the story by the referent of the structure. The clause quoted from 1 Kgs 18:21 shows the people as unresponsive to Elijah’s appeal, and so heightens suspense by suggesting that he may fail to win them over. Narrative prominence is related to “grounding,” and so to the level of transitivity,16 although the nature of the relationship is uncertain.17 However, a prominent structure can occur in any clause, whether foregrounded or backgrounded.18 The significance of “narrative prominence” is, then, more local than that envisaged for “grounding” as currently understood in Biblical Hebrew.19 Like the level of transitivity, narrative prominence is a somewhat indistinct concept, but it can more easily be related to objective criteria. Narrative prominence is, then, the main concern of this study.

The English Detached Participial Clause,” in Discourse Perspectives on Syntax (ed. Flora Klein-Andreu; New York: Academic, 1983): 44-45. The view of “grounding” in biblical narrative referred to is that of R. E. Longacre {Joseph [Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns, 1989]: chapter 3, schematized on p. 81), where a close correlation between grounding and the type of clause used to present the material is envisaged. While generally valid, this probably needs modification. See Longacre’s own questions on perfect verbs (ibid., 82, n. 6) and on negative clauses (idem., “The Discourse Structure of the Flood Narrative,” JAAR 47, Supplement B [1979]: 97). A negated clause does appear to carry forward the action of the narrative in Judg 8:20 as in 1 Kgs 18:21. A “background format” clause in 1 Kgs 20:1, and one of “foreground format” in 2 Kgs 6:24, present virtually the same information, which has specific relevance for the following narrative in the first case, only general relevance in the second. Temporal sequence is characteristic of “foreground,” but the foreground clause beginning 1 Kgs 18:30 moves the action to a point earlier than the “time of the Minhah” of the previous verse, see v. 36. A “foreground format” clause can continue a relative clause (background) as in 1 Kgs 21:4. It seems probable that “grounding” is a highly complex phenomenon, of which “narrative prominence” may be an aspect, but that cannot be argued here.

body.p: 4. Verbs (i) Singular and Plural where the Subject is Preposed.

4.1 Position before the verb of a clause always gives a constituent some prominence, marking it as the “topic” of the clause, or as the “focus” of the narrator’s interest. Clauses in which a collective subject is placed before the verb can, then, provide a suitable test of the possibility that there is a relationship between the treatment of a collective as plural and its prominence in the narrative. Overall (omitting question- able cases), a verb with a preceding collective subject is singular in 17 cases in the corpus, plural in 32. All these cases are treated in §§4.2-4.7.

4.2 A verb following a collective subject is singular where the collective is placed before the verb on account of its intrinsic significance, not on account of its relationship to other items in the context. This occurs where it represents the new information in the answer to a question in
Judg Judah will go up.

Another case in direct speech terminates a speech of prediction, in 2 Sam 17:3 (היהי). The passage is obscure, but the clause appears to give the result of what precedes; it does not contrast with it. Examples occur in narrative where the collective occurs in one of a set of parallel examples which complement each other rather than contrasting, as
Judg Ephraim did not drive out. . .
also (with the same verb) in Judg 1:30,31,33.21

body.p: Here the adverbial refers to the speaker, and the importance of the clause to him (it is a claim for status) appears to be reflected by the choice of the plural verb (cf. §9.3). In 2 Sam 15:11 (וכלה), where a plural verb also follows an adverbial, the 200 unsuspecting men who “accompanied” Absalom must represent, at the very least, a significant depletion of the forces available to David in Jerusalem, explaining the fact that he had no resource but flight (2 Sam 15:14), even if their ignorance of the intended rebellion might make them a doubtful asset to Absalom. This is, then, an incidental clause of considerable interest for the narrative.
body.head: REVELL: LOGIC OF CONCORD
body.p: 4.9 Grammatical features cannot account for the distribution of singular and plural in these verbs which follow a collective subject. As described, the choice of number does correlate with the relative significance of the structure for the narrative—its relative prominence. “Narrative prom- inence” can also account for the choice of number in the few cases where a constituent other than the subject precedes a verb with a collective subject. The interpretation of “prominence” is, of course, often subjective, but the regularity of the pattern shown where the criterion—whether the structure contrasts with what precedes or no—approaches objectivity is a significant support for the view presented here.

5.1 The effects of narrative prominence in other situations can be observed through comparison of clauses with the same verb and the same collective subject. (There are no examples of the same collective subject used with singular and plural forms of the same participle heading the predicate. Examples with similar subjects are given.) Some dozen groups of clauses related in this way can be found, of which the following are typical examples. 5.9 The survey of number in verbs with collective subjects in sections §4 and §5 demonstrates a strong correlation between the use of the plural and high prominence in terms of narrative function. Overall, the head of the predicate is singular in about 60% of the cases where the subject is collective. Singular can, then, be considered the “unmarked” or “default” usage, the form chosen where there is no need to draw special attention to the clause. Plural, the “marked” usage, carries the information that the collective subject, or the clause as a whole, is of particular significance in the narrative. It is a means of drawing attention to the structure comparable to the use of louder or slower enunciation, or to underlining in a written text.

Judg Six hundred men equipped (s.) with weapons.
Judg Six hundred men equipped (pl.) with their weapons.

In Judg 18:11, the information is new, but the significant point of the clause is the origin of the force (it represents the tribe of Dan migrating) not its size or equipment. This is shown by the three adverbials indicating

The size of the force, and its equipment, determines the actions of the main protagonist, the priest. The use of the pronoun in “their weapons” presents the menacing aspect of the force more specifically. The information is presented as new (the article is not used), and so from the viewpoint of the priest, against whom the menace is directed. The use of the plural participle reflects the significance of the phrase in this situation. Judg 18:17 shows the priest standing by while his shrine is plundered. “The 600 men equipped with weapons” (part of the compound subject) are presented as old information (with anaphoric article) as a reminder of the reason for his action. In 9:36, the speaker makes a casual observation on people at such a distance that his companion can reasonably suggest that what he has seen is only shadows on the mountains. The plural is used in 1 Kgs 20:30 in a clause describing the miraculous destruction of those remaining (27,000) from an immense hostile force. Both attributive and verb are plural in Judg 18:16, 1 Sam 14:22 and 2 Sam 15:11. The clause in these cases is sufficiently significant to be marked as prominent by the plural verb. The subject itself is also prominent. It denotes a menace in Judg 18:16 (see §6.3), a significant group of allies in 1 Sam 14:22 (see §6.2), and a similarly significant group in 2 Sam 15:11 (see §4.8). Where the attributive is singular and the head of the predicate plural, the attributive presents a characteristic: “equipped” (רוגח Judg 18:11); “chosen” (רוחב Judg 20:34); “large” (2 בר Sam 13:34); also the temporary characteristic “going out” (1 אצי Sam 17:20). The group designated by these collectives is not significant beyond the function of actor in its immediate context (on Judg 18:11, see §6.3), so that a singular attributive is expected (see §6.1). The verb presents mainline narrative in Judg 18:11 and 20:34. In 1 Sam 17:20, the clause presents a significant incident, consequently the verb is plural (see §4.7). The situation in 2 Sam 13:34 “A large (s.) people travelling (pl.)” is similar. The approach of the group is significant in the narrative context, so the use of the plural is justified (see §5.8.2). 6.7 The predicate is singular and the attributive plural in
body.p: 1 Kgs The people were camping against Gibbethon . . . and the people camping (pl.) heard (s.)...

The initial plural predicate “were camping” presumably highlights the contrast between the relative positions of the king—in the capital—and the people (i.e., the army)—on campaign. The army is thus not under the king’s control, and so is able to set up its commander as a rival to him. The continued use of the plural in the attributive “camping” may simply be due to attraction, but it may be intended to highlight the significance of this group of people for the event described. The use of a singular verb no doubt reflects the fact that the clause is relatively low in transitivity, and presents an event which is effectively background to the more significant crowning of the king described in the next clause (see §7.3). The situation is similar in 2 Sam 19:4, where the plural attributive םימלכנה heightens the simile likening David’s victorious troops to “people disgraced by defeat,” carrying on the theme of “victory turned to defeat” begun in 2 Sam 19:3. The singular verb בנגתי “steals away” reflects the fact that the clause is of no significance for the ongoing narrative.

6.8 As described, then, an adjective, participle, or demonstrative at- tributive to a collective is typically singular. This is the “unmarked” situation. The use of the plural, which contrasts with this, generally correlates with particular significance in the narrative. That is, the “marked” use indicates narrative prominence. It is also true that adjectives and participles which denote an enduring quality or characteristic of the collective modified are almost invariably singular (as are demonstratives), while the participles of active verbs in other uses are more frequently plural. That is, the correlation of singular with stative/passive/reflexive value and plural with action noted in §2.2 is evident here. This shows that the level of transitivity was a significant factor in the choice of number in attributives. This could be considered as a separate factor, or as an aspect of what is called here “narrative prominence,” a question discussed in §9.2. The information given in §§6.6, 6.7, shows that the factors which determine the choice of number in an attributive are independent of those which determine the choice of number in a verb. This conclusion is confirmed in §8.2.

body.p: 7. Other Coreferents of Collective Subjects

7.1 This section surveys the choice of number in pronouns, other than that in the verb, which are coreferent with a collective subject. The term “verb” is used in this section with the meaning “head of the predicate.” The few cases where a collective subject is marked for number by a participle or other nominal acting as head of the predicate are included. The general rule is that, when the collective is marked as plural, following coreferents are typically also plural. Where the collective is marked as singular, coreferents in the same clause (or in clauses subordinate to it) are usually singular. Otherwise they are plural. Coref­ erent pronouns in other following clauses are typically plural. Usage contrasting with these “unmarked” situations appears to carry a semantic load.
The collective is marked as plural.

7.2 Where a collective is subject of a plural verb, a coreferent is typically plural. In most of the exceptions noted, the singular coreferent can be understood as distributive in value; there is ellipsis of שיא ‘man/each’ which is typically used in the distributive structure, as
Judg All that generation was gathered (pl.) {each} to his fathers.

The same occurs in Judg 20:33 “All the men of Israel rose (pl.) {each} from his place” (ומוקממ); also probably in the subordinate clause in 1 Sam 13:6 “The men of Israel saw (pl.) {each} that he was in distress” יכ רצ ול ); and possibly in the descriptive clause in Judg 20:17 “The ( men of Israel gathered (pl.) . . .; {each one} of these ( ) was a warrior.” Further examples of pronouns which may have distributive value are given in §8.4. In Judg 1:34, “he did not allow him,” the subject, “he,” is coreferent with a collective subject treated as plural, the object, “him,” with a plural nominal. It seems likely that the text has been disturbed.

7.3 Where a collective is subject of a singular verb, a coreferent pronoun in the same clause, or in a clause subordinate to it, is usually singular. In such cases, the clause is typically low in narrative prom- inence and transitivity, as
Sam Aram saw (s.) that it was driven back before Israel.

Here the subordinate clause presents the motivation for a new mobilization of the forces of Aram. It is introductory to a description of the activities of their leader, which are of interest only as indicating David’s problems. Thus the clause is low in narrative prominence. In addition, the clause is intransitive. A plural coreferent is used in situations high in narrative prominence or transitivity, as
body.head: 1 Kgs All Israel saw (s.) that the king did not listen to them.
body.p: Here the clause is also introductory, but it presents the immediate cause of the division of the kingdom, and so is central to the narrator’s concerns, and high in narrative prominence. The clause is negative, but transitive. The plural is also used in Judg 2:10 (ועדי, presenting a defect in the people which is crucial to the narrative), Judg 7:2 (םדיב, in a clause which presents the motivation for the reduction in the strength of Gideon’s force), Judg 20:39 (ורמא, presenting the thought which determines Ben- jamin’s disastrous action), 2 Sam 19:4 (םסונב, highlighting the theme of victory turned to defeat, as the preceding םימלכנ, see §6.7), and 2 Kgs 17:19 (םהיהלא, where the plural highlights the fact that the essential obedience to God was abandoned). The final case, םתולעב (Judg 11:16), is difficult to evaluate, as it is the only example of a pronoun of this sort preceding the collective and its verb. The use of the plural is possibly anomalous (cf. the singular suffix on the infinitive used in the same context, but following the verb, in Judg 11:13).

9. Conclusion.

9.1 This survey shows that, generally speaking, the choice of number in coreferents of the collectives in the corpus follows regular patterns. Where the collective is subject of a clause, the head of the predicate is generally singular, as are other coreferents within the clause, and in clauses subordinate to it. More distant coreferents, outside the syntactic unit formed by the clause, are generally plural. Where a collective does not act as subject, coreferents are also usually plural; the singular is common only within the same constituent as the collective. A nominal attributive to a collective is generally singular, but this also has no effect on other relationships within the clause. Where singular is expected, the use of the plural is mainly determined by the prominence of the collective or its clause in the narrative. Other factors, particularly high transitivity, and the fact that the collective is actor, are also conducive to the use of the plural. Certain passages, characterized above as “histor­ ical synopsis” or “prophetic register,” use an unusually high proportion of singular cjoreferents. Outside these passages, the proportion of exam­ ples which must be described as anomalies, in that they clearly conflict with the common pattern, is negligible.

“Narrative prominence” is a form of “grounding,” and so related 9.2 to the level of transitivity (see §3.4). The two factors which mainly determine the use of the plural can, then, be seen as aspects of a single factor, for which the term “immediacy” seems appropriate. Material which is prominent in the narrative is “immediate” in the sense that it is central to the narrator’s purpose. Narrative is concerned with a series of

This is no doubt the basis for the correlation between function as sub­ ject—as “actor”—and the use of the plural noted in §2.2. This phenome­ non was associated with transitivity in §2 and §3, but it seems quite probable that the level of transitivity is, in this context, simply a measure of the degree of “action” significant to the narrative.

9.3 The use of concord to mark structure as prominent or significant in the narrative has a parallel in direct speech, where concord in person is one of several features used to mark significance in terms of the purpose or concerns of the speaker. Where deference is required, defer­ ential nominals or other third person forms are used to refer to speaker and addressee. First or second person pronouns express “immediacy”; their use reflects the strong concern or emotion of the speaker. Concord with collectives is, then, part of a network of features used throughout the language to show that a structure is “immediate”—particularly sig­ nificant in its context, or “non-immediate”—distanced, background, and relatively unimportant.

9.4 Thus the choice of singular in a verb with a collective subject does correspond to the common conventions of grammar, but this “un­ marked” or “default” form is used because the situation does not require the use of the plural to mark immediacy. The use of the plural may show that the referent of the collective is viewed as a number of individ­ uals, but its use is determined by the need to mark the immediacy of the structure. The increased use of the singular in passages of historical synopsis is consistent with this. The narrative in Judges chapters 1, 11:13-21, and 20, is mainly concerned with political actions. No leaders or rulers are named (save in the Caleb story in Judg 1:12-15 = Josh 15:16-19); the actions are viewed abstractly, as undertaken by population groups seen as “states.” In more vivid narrative passages, such political actions are typically depicted as performed by the leader of the group treated as an individual, whether named alone, as in 2 Sam 8:1, or as head of a compound treated as singular, as in 1 Sam 23:5. In the three passages of historical synopsis, the narrator presents the political struggles as background to the narrative of those aspects of the history of Israel

9.6 The language of Qumran represents a late stage in the development of the tendency to treat collectives as plural. The usage of the corpus, where collectives are treated as singular in their primary syntactic rela­ tionships in 60% of the cases, represents an earlier stage. Presumably, in yet earlier stages, the singular was even more frequently used. It is possible that successive generations of the ancients viewed the increasing use of the plural as progressive abandonment of “classical” grammar for “vulgar” usage, as was the tendency among more recent grammarians. From another point of view, however, it represents the increasing ex­ ploitation of a development which made use of spare morphosyntactic capacity. In other words it is an example of one of the ways in which the expressive capabilities of languages are developed.

body.p: 1. Introduction

This paper attempts to assign a value to the use of ינא and יכנא, the two forms of free (independent) first person pronoun used in bibli- cal Hebrew. The general opinion is that they are free variants (see Waltke-O’Connor [1990], 16.3). In the discussion of the origin of the two forms in Aartun (1971) it is suggested that the longer form was developed from the shorter by the addition of an enclitic mark- ing emphasis. However, if יכנא did have an emphatic function in contrast to ינא, it had lost it by the time the biblical text was fixed as we know it. H.B. Rosen (1984) suggested that the two forms differ in some features of usage, but the pattern which he found in the Pentateuch does not fit other books well.1 Consequently there is room for a new attempt to elucidate the question on a wider basis.2

The present study sets out to describe the use of ינא and יכנא in those prose materials in which both forms commonly appear. The Book of Deuteronomy and the parts of the Pentateuch assigned to P are not included, since here the two forms are used in proportions quite differ- ent from those found in the other parts of the Pentateuch.3 The corpus

A free pronoun in apposition to a bound one is superfluous to structure and basic content. body.head: 3.2 Emotion
body.p: A claim is typically put forward with some emotion, reflecting the speaker’s personal interest. ינא is similarly used in other cases in which non-status speakers speak with particular feeling, as in ‘Bless me too, father’ (Esau appealing to his father after Jacob has fore- stalled him, Gen. 27:34, 38); ‘I, where am I to go?’ (Reuben, discov- ering the loss of Joseph, whom he had tried to protect, Gen. 37:30); ‘Have you even brought misfortune on the widow with whom I am staying?’ (Elijah, impatient with the trials of his life, 1 Kgs 17:20); ‘I left prosperous, and the Lord has brought me back destitute’ (Naomi’s bitter reflection on the meaning of her name, Ruth 1:21). In Gen. 41:9 Pharaoh’s butler uses ינא in confessing his oversight; Micah also uses ינא in his confession in Judg. 17:2, as does Shimei in 2 Sam. 19:21, and Abigail in accepting blame, and excusing herself in 1 Sam. 25:24, 25.14 Other examples of the use of ינא by non-sta- tus speakers reflecting emotion occur in 2 Sam. 11:11 (Uriah is astonished at David’s suggestion); 2 Sam. 13:13 (Tamar is horrified by that of her brother); 1 Kgs 1:21, 26 (Bathsheba and Nathan are anxious about the future); 1 Kgs 19:10, 14 (Elijah expresses to God his feeling of isolation); also 1 Kgs 3:17; 18:12 (see 3.3.1). There is in Judg. 19:18, but, if הוהי uncertainty over the meaning of it does give the speaker’s final destination, as seems probable, his use of ינא may reasonably be regarded as emotional.

14 Clauses confessing, or accepting blame, (damaging to the speaker’s self esteem or positive face wants, Brown and Levinson [1987], 68) are typically pre- sented with first person pronouns, reflecting emotion, not with deferential forms, where the speech as a whole is deferential, or where deferential speech might be expected (as Jos. 7:20; 1 Sam. 12:19; 2 Sam. 14:9; 24:10). The same is true in the clauses intended to justify the speaker’s conduct, as in the cases 1 Sam. 25:24, 25; also in 1 Sam. 1:1516־; and ‘My servant tricked me’ (2 Sam. 19:27).
body.head: REDUNDANCY OR EXPRESSIVE CONTRAST
body.p: 3.2.1 A non-status speaker may use ינא or יכנא in a clause of self- identification, (a clause with a first person singular pronoun as sub- ject, and a phrase which designates the speaker by name or social position, or by relationship to other individuals, or groups, or even to events, as predicate). ינא is used in Gen. 27:24, where Jacob asserts for a second time (in response to his father’s evident suspicion), that he is Esau, and in Gen. 27:32, where Esau responds to his father’s question ‘Who are you?’ — a question which Esau’s preceding speech should have rendered unnecessary. ינא is also used by Hannah in 1 Sam. 1:26 where she identifies herself to Eli by recalling their former meeting. In all three cases, the speech is of unusual impor- tance to the speaker. Jacob must prevent discovery of his deception; Esau must prove his identity in the face of unexpected scepticism. Hannah’s strong interest in her speech is evident from her use of two vocatives and a formula of asseveration to introduce it. The use of ינא can, then, be seen as reflecting emotion. Where such strong feeling is not reflected, a non-status speaker uses יכנא in clauses of this sort, as does Jacob where he first introduces himself with ‘I am Esau your firstborn’ in Gen. 27:19.15
body.head: 3.3 Emphasis
body.p: In other cases the use of ינא seems to have no connotations beyond the desire to draw attention to the pronoun. It is used to emphasize the actions of the speaker in contrast to those of others, as in ‘Give him into my care, and I will bring him back to you’ (Gen. 42:37; other examples occur in Gen. 33:14; Judg. 1:3; 8:23; 1 Sam. 17:9; 2 Sam. 12:28; 17:15; 1 Kgs 1:14; 21:7). ינא is similarly used to highlight a shift of the topic to the speaker’s own situation, as in ‘I too was in my dream’ (Gen. 40:16; other examples occur in Gen. 24:45; Judg. 20:4; 1 Sam. 17:28; also ‘And I said..’ Ruth 4:4). The speaker uses ינא in the forceful (or emotional) presenta­

15 יכנא also precedes a personal name acting as predicate in Ruth 3:9, a descrip- tive phrase designating an individual in 1 Sam. 4:16, 9:19, a phrase indicating that the speaker is related to another individual, or is a member of a group in Gen. 24:24, 34; Judg. 17:9; 1 Sam. 30:13; 2 Sam. 1:8, 13. In pragmatic terms, these clauses indicate the place of the speaker in the community, i.e. they identify the speaker. Cf. the form in which identification is requested in Gen. 24:23; 1 Sam. 17:58. The choice of P-S order is more likely to represent a form of self-effacement or distancing than to mark identification of this sort as categorically different from a more specific identification (only meaningful when the speaker is well-known), since S-P order is used for either of the meaning categories recognized by Muraoka (1985), 7-8, and Waltke-O’Connor (1990), 8.4a.

In Gen. 31:44, 52 (Laban making arrangements with Jacob); Exodus 33:16 (twice; Moses pleading with God); Num. 20:19 (Israel making arrangements with Moab); Judg. 12:2 (Jephthah justifying himself to Ephraim). In other examples, the use of יבא seems intended to mark the clause in question as crucial to the situation. Pharaoh’s butler uses יבא in the clause in which he states that he and the baker had dreams (Gen. 41:11; the speech informs Pharaoh that Joseph, who interpreted those dreams, is the man Pharaoh wants). In 1 Sam. 4:16, the messenger intro- duces himself with יכבא, as is expected, ‘I am the one who came from the battle’, but uses יבא in pointing out that his news is fresh, and grave, ‘I fled from the battle today’. Similarly, lookouts use יבא in reporting significant developments in 2 Sam. 18:27; 2 Kgs 9:17. Samson’s use of יבא in Judg. 15:3 is presumably a further example.

3.3.1 יכבא is used where such emphasis is not required. It is used in clauses which are not central to the main concern of the speech, which provide ‘background’ in various ways. Thus clauses which introduce a speech by providing a context against which what follows is to be understood most commonly show יכבא, as Sarah’s statement ‘I gave my servant into your bosom’ (where the topic of the speech is the occurrence described in what follows: Gen. 16:5). Other examples occur in Gen. 24:13; Exod. 7:17; Judg. 7:17; 1 Kgs 2:2, 16, 20. The use of יבא in introductory clauses of this sort by the harlot in 1 Kgs 3:17, and by Obadiah in 1 Kgs 18:12, reflects strong emotion, as is shown by their speech. יכבא is similarly used in clauses which add ancillary detail within a section of narrative, as in Gen. 28:16, ‘(Surely God is in this place) and I did not know’. Other examples occur in Judg. 19:18 (also 1 Sam. 18:23; Ruth 2:10; see 3.1.1). The speech of the prophet to the queen (as an equal) in 1 Kgs 14:6 should probably be included here. In contrast, יבא is used in such clauses where the detail added is particularly significant, as in Gen. 18:13, ‘I being old’, presented by Sarah as an insuperable obstacle to child-bear- ing, or the claim ‘I being a great people’ put forward in Jos. 17:14 (see 3.1).

body.head: 4.1 Status-marked Use of^^ for Self Effacement
body.p: Where a status-marked speaker, for whom ינא is the standard, unmarked form, uses יכנא, the clause sometimes indicates the speak- er’s relative lack of importance. This is clearest where Jonathan says to David, his subordinate, ‘I will be second to you (1 Sam. 23:17).19 Another case occurs in 2 Sam. 3:39, ‘Today I am weak’, where David explains his inability to control the Bene Zeruiah. In 2 Sam. 7:2, ‘I am living in a palace of cedar’, David contrasts his luxurious situa­

He has previously used ינא in addressing David (1 Sam. 19:3, 3; 20:20, 23). Joshua has rhetorically abandoned his position as leader and has offered the people a free choice between the God of their fathers and the gods of the heathen. His use of יכנא, presenting himself as one of the people, heightens the impact of this effective termination to his speech. David’s use of יכנא in 2 Sam. 15:28, ‘I will linger...’, probably reflects the feeling that he has lost his kingdom to Absalom, and so is without status.20

body.head: 4.3 Background
body.p: יכנא is also used by status-marked speakers in clauses which do not present the main concern of the speech, but are introductory or oth- erwise ancillary to the main concern. In 2 Sam. 3:13, ‘I just want to ask one thing...’ (and similarly in 2 Sam. 14:18), David uses יכנא in a clause which introduces a request, but does not make it. Israel uses יכנא to Joseph in ‘I am about to die’ (Gen. 48:21), which provides information in the context of which what follows is to be under- stood. Similar usage by others occurs in Gen. 50:5, Jos. 23:14. Pharaoh’s use of יכנא in ‘I will send you away’ (Exod. 8:24) similarly appears to mark this concession as unimportant in comparison to the instructions which it introduces. ינא is used in an introductory clause of this sort in ‘I and the people with me will approach...’ (Jos. 8:5) where Joshua is issuing instructions for the attack on Ai, so that the content is of greater significance to the speaker. ינא is also used in ‘I am old, advanced in years’ in Jos. 23:2, and similarly in 1 Sam. 12:2, where exhortation to the people as a whole is introduced. The situa- tion is thus of greater general significance than those in which יכנא is used in introductory statements of impending death.24

5. ינא and יכנא in Human Speech, Conclusions

Where the use of ינא and יכנא is classified in terms of the status of the speaker relative to the addressee, a regular pattern appears. This is clearest where the speaker is status-marked. Such speakers typically use ינא. They use יכנא in little more than quarter of the possible cases. They can use it to show that the status difference between the mem- bers of the dyad is being ignored to influence the addressee, to show humility or politeness, or to show that the clause functions as ‘back- ground’. Non-status speakers usually use יכנא, but use ינא in over one third of the cases. It is used to put forward a claim of some sort, an obvious counterpart to the use of יכנא by a status-marked speaker showing humility. The use of ינא by a non-status speaker often reflects emotion or strong feeling, a similar usage since this also draws the speaker’s concerns forcefully to the attention of the addressee. The use of ינא by non-status speakers to mark a clause as significant is the counterpart to the use of יכנא by status-marked speakers to show that a clause is background. The most common situation in which ינא is used in this category, to heighten a contrast or other shift in topic, is characteristically marked by other ‘foregrounding’ devices in other situations: the use of a subject placed before the verb, of a free pronominal subject in a verbal clause, etc. Thus, although the recognition of any particular clause as ‘significant’ is, in isolation, arbitrary, comparison of usage can supply considerable support for such recognition. The use of ינא and יכנא by human speakers can, then, be seen as a self-consistent system which corresponds, on occa- sion, to features of other systems with similar functions.
In general, then, the use of ינא by humans shows either that the speaker is status-marked, or that the clause is ‘immediate’, is central
body.head: REDUNDANCY OR EXPRESSIVE CONTRAST
body.p: to the interests of the speaker, or the addressee, or both. The use of יכנא marks the speaker as non-status, or shows that the clause is ‘non-immediate’, peripheral to the speaker’s concerns, unimpor- tant. Relative status and degree of personal concern are not really distinct alternatives. The concerns of a status-marked speaker are perforce of interest to an addressee of lower status. The concerns of a non-status speaker can only be presented to a superior as ‘imme- diate’ where the speaker’s emotion, or feeling of urgency, overrides respect for the addressee’s status. Several other features are used in a similar way. The position of the vocative, and the opposition between personal pronouns and deferential forms, have a range of function similar to that suggested for these pronoun forms (see 2.1-2). The treatment of a collective as plural marks the clause of which it is subject as central to the concerns of the speaker or nar- rator; the treatment of it as singular marks it as non-central (see Revell [1993b]). There is, then, a considerable network of features used to mark the relative significance of individual clauses, a network which supplements the information provided by the grammatical marking of foreground and background (see n. 6). The two forms of first person singular pronoun are used as part of this network.
6. Speech Ascribed to God
body.head: 6.1 The Use of יכנא
body.p: 6.1.1 God is represented as using יכנא where the speech concerns the addressee on a personal level. Such speech often offers protection or other support, or expresses kindness, as ‘Do not fear, Abraham, I am a shield for you’ (Gen. 15:1; other uses after the comforting ‘Do not fear’ occur in Gen. 26:24; 46:4 [twice]; Jos. 11:6). Other exam- pies are ‘I will be with your mouth’ (to Moses, Exod. 4:12, and sim- ilarly 4:15); ‘I will let you know what you should do’ (to Samuel, 1 Sam. 16:3); ‘I have heard’ (accepting the repentance of Josiah, 2 Kgs 22:19). ‘Was it not I, the Lord?’ (Exod. 4:11) can be associated with this group, since the clause, which depicts God’s power as creator, begins a speech expressing support for Moses (cf. Exod 4:12). Simi- larly ‘I (יכנא) will make a covenant’ (Exod. 34:10) responds to Moses’ request for support in v. 9. Other examples occur in Gen. 28:15; Exod 19:9; 23:20; 34:11; Jos. 13:6; 1 Sam. 24:4. יכנא is also used in clauses in which God identifies himself through his relation- ship to the ancestors of the addressee, as ‘I am the God of Abraham your father’ (Gen. 26:24; also Gen. 46:3; Exod. 3:6), or through an

body.p: event in which the addressee has participated in ‘I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a monument...’ (Gen. 31:13).

6.1.2 יכנא is also used in speech by God in clauses which are ‘back- ground’ in that they establish a context in which what follows is to be understood, or are otherwise introductory to a speech, as ‘In yet seven days I will bring rain... (and I will wipe out...)’ (Gen. 7:4); ‘I shall do something in Israel...’ (1 Sam. 3:11); ‘I brought Israel up from Egypt...’ (1 Sam. 10:18; and similarly Judg. 6:8). Other exam- pies occur in Gen. 20:6 (twice); Exod. 3:12; 7:27; Jos. 1:2; 2 Sam. 12:7; 24:12. In ‘I will also judge the nation which they will serve’ (Gen. 15:14), ‘I will kill your firstborn’ (Exod. 4:23, where God tells Moses how to address Pharaoh when he reaches Egypt), יכנא is used in a clause presenting an intended future action which is remote. Such usage is possibly to be seen as ‘distancing’ and so marking as unimportant, a parallel to ‘background’ usage.
body.head: 6.2 The Use of ינא
body.p: ינא is usually used, in speech ascribed to God, in clauses which do not refer to the addressee, as ‘Am I (ינא) going to hide from Abra- ham what I (ינא) am going to do?’ (Gen. 18:17, Abraham is not addressed); ‘I have hardened his heart’ (Exod. 10:1); ‘At midnight I will go out through Egypt...;’ (Exod. 11:4), ‘I have rejected him’ (1 Sam. 16:1); ‘I will be a father to him’ (2 Sam. 7:14). Other examples occur in Exod. 4:21; Exod. 9:14 (presented as instruction to Moses, not as speech to Pharaoh); Judg. 2:21; 1 Sam. 3:13; 2 Sam. 7:8 (spoken to Nathan, not to David). The oath formula As I live’ ( Num. 14:21) can be added. Where a second person pronoun is used in the clause, the addressee is scarcely involved, as ‘I know that he will not allow you...’ (Exod. 3:19); ‘For what I am going to do for you is awesome’ (Exod. 34:10, the ‘doing’ is intended as a sign to the people); ‘Your eyes will not see the mis- fortune I am going to bring’ (2 Kgs 22:20). In 2 Sam. 12:12 ‘I (ינא) will do this thing before all Israel...’ there is no use of the sec- ond person in the clause, but it does closely concern the addressee, David. ינא is possibly used to heighten the contrast with the pre- ceding clause (see 3.3). The cases in Exod. 33:19 and 1 Sam. 23:4 appear to be anomalies (cf. 1 Sam. 24:4). ינא is also used in clauses of self-identification in which the name הוהי ‘the Lord’ is used, even where reference is made to the addressee, as in Gen. 15:7, ‘I am the Lord who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldees...’ Other examples occur in Gen. 28:13; Exod. 7:17; 10:2; Judg.

body.p: 6:10; 1 Kgs 20:13, 28. The use of יכנא with this name in Exod. 20:2, 5 is exceptional.

The use of יכנא usual in speech directed by God to a human can be interpreted as the sort of condescension shown by a status-marked human who uses יכנא as a form of politeness (4.2). The fact that such usage is rare with humans, usual with God, may reflect the fact that God’s status is never in doubt, whereas human status may be questioned, and so is constantly asserted. It seems quite likely that, in this feature, the speech of God may reflect that of human parents, who are unlikely (as usage in other languages, such as French and German, suggests) to use status language to small children. יכנא is also used in speech ascribed to God, as in that of status-marked humans, to mark clauses as ‘background’. יבא is used where the use of יכנא is not required for the purposes described. Thus the use of יבא and יכבא in speech by God can be explained as based on the same concepts as in speech by humans.26 However, speech ascribed to God does seem to contain more anomalies in the use of these forms than is the case with human speech.
7. The Wider Context
body.head: 7.1 Biblical Hebrew
body.p: A set of distinguishing features allows the division of biblical Hebrew into an early’ form (EBH) and a ‘late’ form (LBH). In LBH, the only first person singular pronoun form used is יבא, as is the case in all later Hebrew (apart from quotation or imitation of the biblical language). The ‘P’ material of the Pentateuch (the characteristics of which are carefully studied in Hurwitz [1982]) represents LBH; the failure to use יכבא is characteristic of it. In the Book of Deuteron- omy, which represents EBH, יכבא is far more common than יבא, but the bulk of the examples occur in speech by God (transmitted through Moses), and so are consistent with the usage of the corpus (6.1), as are other uses of first person singular forms generally. The few anomalies are insufficient to support a claim that the usage in Deuteronomy has a different basis from that of the corpus. The rest of the Bible — those parts of the Latter Prophets and Writings which show the use of both יבא and יכבא typical of EBH — is written in a

body.p: variety of poetical styles. In some sections, such as Psalm 119, and the Book of Job, usage can be aligned with that of the corpus. Other parts show some similarities. Thus, speakers other than God use יכנא for self-identification or description (Isa. 6:5; Jer. 1:6, 7; Amos 7:14; Jonah 1:9; Zech. 13:5), except where the clause represents self-asser- tion (Isa. 19:11; 47:8, 10), or emotion (Isa. 49:21). There are also differences. Thus God often uses יכנא in identifying himself as הוהי (as in Isa. 44:24; 51:15; Hos. 12:10; 13:4). In general, then, usage in poetical materials differs from that of the corpus.
body.head: 7.2 Other Semitic Languages
body.p: In so far as we know their languages, the peoples surrounding the earlier biblical Israel used cognates of יכנא, not cognates of ינא (Garr [1985], 79-80).27 Cognates of both appear in Akkadian and Phoeni- cian (see Aartun [1971]) but their use is marginal. The biblical usage finds its only real parallel in Ugaritic, where a long form, ank, cog- nate with יכנא, is used in texts of all kinds, and a short form, an, cog- nate with ינא, is limited to poetic texts, in which both forms are used with no evident difference in function (Segert [1984], 58; for the examples see Whitaker [1972]). Ugaritic poetry has well-known affinities of style and vocabulary with biblical poetry, one being the use of pairs of synonyms, one common, the other often uncommon in the language as a whole, in the production of the characteristic parallelism. The two forms of first person pronoun are occasionally used in parallel in this way, as in
םימש יכנא I made the earth... My hands spread out the heavens (Isa. 45:12).
ץרא ... ינא
A Ugaritic example occurs in text 4[51] .4, lines 5960־.

As with the Icelandic Sagas, material from different periods has no doubt been used. However the language of the corpus is generally homogeneous. Epigraphic material dated c. 600 BCE includes an idiom and an oath formula used in the biblical description of events from the same period, and shows no significant differences from the Ian- guage of the corpus other than orthographic. body.head: REDUNDANCY OR EXPRESSIVE CONTRAST
body.p: were evidently brought into general use in Hebrew, where ינא Func- tioned as a marked form. Its contrast with יכנא achieves a form of what is called ‘responsibility indexing’ by Mühlhäusler and Harre (1990), 92ff.: the marking of the speaker’s position in a moral order or rights and duties of speaking and of acting through speaking. The use of ינא shows that the speaker has a right to expect attention from the addressee, either due to status difference, or due to the importance of the speech for the speaker. The fact that ינא, the marked form, eventually replaced the unmarked may result from excessive use in the effort to speak expressively (for other possible examples in Hebrew see Revell [1993b], 9.5 and n. 34); or some social development such as that which appears to have led to the use of you’ in place of contrast- ing thou’ and you’ in address to an individual in English. The devel- opment was no doubt hastened by the similarity of ינא to the first per- son pronoun of Aramaic, increasingly common as a second language for Hebrew speakers as the biblical period progressed. The fact that יכנא, and so the marking of the speaker’s status, was abandoned at such a relatively early date may well reflect the social upheaval brought about by the capture of Jerusalem by the Babylonians in 597 BCE, which resulted in the abolition of the monarchy, and the transporta- tion to Babylonia, or flight elsewhere, of many Hebrew speakers.
